paragraphs: There is only one country on earth where citizens enjoy unlimited freedom of association for political purposes. This same country is the only one in the world where the constant exercise of the right of association has been carried into civil life, and where all the advantages that civilization can offer are obtained through it. In every country where political associations are forbidden, civil associations are rare. It is hardly likely that this is an accident. We should rather infer that there is a natural, and perhaps a necessary, connection between these two kinds of associations. Certain men happen to share an interest in some matter. Perhaps a commercial undertaking is to be managed, or some manufacturing venture to be tried. They meet and combine, and in this way they gradually become familiar with the principle of association. The more numerous the small affairs are, the more men acquire, without even knowing it, the skill to carry out great undertakings together. Civil associations therefore make political association easier. But political association, on the other hand, remarkably strengthens and improves associations for civil purposes. In civil life every man may, strictly speaking, imagine that he can provide for his own needs. In politics he can imagine nothing of the kind. When a people has any knowledge of public life, then, the idea of association and the wish to unite occur every day to the whole community. Whatever natural reluctance may keep men from acting together, they will always be ready to combine for the sake of a party. Political life thus makes the love and practice of association more general. It gives a desire for union, and teaches the means of combining, to numbers of men who would otherwise have lived apart all their lives.

Politics gives birth not only to numerous associations but to associations on a large scale. In civil life it seldom happens that any single interest draws a very large number of men to act together, and much skill is needed to bring such an interest into being. In politics, however, opportunities arise every day. Now it is only in great associations that the general value of the principle of association shows itself. Citizens who are individually powerless do not clearly foresee the strength they could gain by uniting. It must be shown to them before they can understand it. Hence it is often easier to gather a multitude for a public purpose than a few people. A thousand citizens do not see what interest they have in combining, but ten thousand will see it perfectly well. In politics men combine for great undertakings, and the use they make of the principle of association in important affairs teaches them in practice that it is in their interest to help each other in smaller ones. A political association draws a number of individuals out of their own circle all at once. However much age, mind, and fortune may naturally keep them apart, it brings them closer together and puts them in contact. Once they have met, they can always meet again.

Men can enter few civil partnerships without risking part of their possessions. This is the case with all manufacturing and trading companies. When men are still little practiced in the art of association and do not know its main rules, they are afraid, the first time they combine in this way, of paying dearly for their experience. They therefore prefer to do without a powerful instrument of success rather than run the risks that come with using it. They are less reluctant, however, to join political associations, which seem to them free of danger because they risk no money in them. But they cannot belong to these associations for long without discovering how order is kept among a large number of men, and by what means they are made to advance toward the same object in a harmonious and methodical way. In this way they learn to surrender their own will to the will of all the rest, and to make their own efforts subordinate to the common impulse. These things are just as necessary to know in civil associations as in political ones. Political associations may therefore be seen as large free schools, where all the members of the community go to learn the general theory of association.

But even if political association did not directly contribute to the progress of civil association, destroying the former would still damage the latter. When citizens may meet in public only for certain purposes, they regard such meetings as a strange proceeding that rarely happens, and they hardly think about it at all. When they are allowed to meet freely for every purpose, they come to look on public association as the universal means, and in a way the only means, that men can use to accomplish the various purposes they have in view. Every new need immediately brings the idea back to mind. The art of association then becomes, as I have said before, the mother of action, studied and applied by all.

When some kinds of associations are prohibited and others allowed, it is hard to tell the first from the second in advance. In this state of doubt men avoid associations altogether, and a kind of public opinion takes hold that tends to make any association whatever seem a bold and almost illegal enterprise. *a

[Footnote a: This is especially true when the executive government has discretionary power to allow or prohibit associations. When certain associations are simply prohibited by law, and the courts of justice have to punish violations of that law, the harm is far less considerable. Every citizen then knows fairly well beforehand what to expect. He judges himself before the law judges him, and, avoiding the prohibited associations, he joins those the law permits. It is by such restrictions that all free nations have always admitted that the right of association might be limited. But suppose the legislature were to give a man the power to decide beforehand which associations are dangerous and which are useful, and to authorize him either to destroy all associations in the bud or to allow them to form. Since nobody could foresee in what cases associations might be established and in what cases they would be put down, the spirit of association would be entirely paralyzed. The first of these laws would attack only certain associations; the second would apply to society itself and do it harm. I can conceive that a regular government may resort to the first, but I do not grant that any government has the right to enact the second.]

It is therefore an unrealistic fantasy to suppose that the spirit of association, when it is suppressed on one point, will still show the same vigor on all others. It is equally one to suppose that if men are allowed to pursue certain undertakings in common, that is enough to make them take them up eagerly. When the members of a community are allowed and accustomed to combine for all purposes, they will combine as readily for the smaller ones as for the more important. But if they are allowed to combine only for small affairs, they will be neither inclined nor able to do it. It is in vain that you leave them entirely free to carry on their business as joint-stock companies. They will hardly care to use the rights you have granted them. And after you have exhausted your strength in vain efforts to put down the prohibited associations, you will be surprised that you cannot persuade men to form the associations you encourage.

I do not say that there can be no civil associations in a country where political association is prohibited, for men can never live in society without engaging in some common undertakings. But I maintain that in such a country civil associations will always be few in number, feebly planned, and unskillfully managed. They will never form any vast designs, or they will fail in carrying them out.

This naturally leads me to think that freedom of association in political matters is not as dangerous to public tranquility as is supposed. It may even be that, after stirring up society for some time, it strengthens the state in the end. In democratic countries, political associations are, so to speak, the only powerful persons who aspire to rule the state. The governments of our time accordingly look on such associations as the sovereigns of the Middle Ages looked on the great vassals of the crown. They feel a kind of instinctive abhorrence of them and combat them on every occasion. They feel, on the contrary, a natural goodwill toward civil associations, because they readily see that these institutions, instead of directing the minds of the community toward public affairs, divert them from such reflections. By engaging men more and more in the pursuit of objects that cannot be attained without public tranquility, civil associations deter them from revolutions. But these governments overlook the fact that political associations amazingly multiply and ease those of a civil character, and that in avoiding a dangerous evil they deprive themselves of an effective remedy.

When you see the Americans freely and constantly forming associations to promote some political principle, to raise one man to the head of affairs, or to take power away from another, you have some difficulty understanding why men so independent do not constantly fall into the abuse of freedom. If, on the other hand, you look at the endless number of trading companies operating in the United States, and see that the Americans are everywhere unceasingly engaged in carrying out important and difficult plans, which the slightest revolution would throw into confusion, you will readily understand why people so well occupied are not at all tempted to disturb the state or to destroy the public tranquility from which they all profit.

Is it enough to observe these things separately? Should we not discover the hidden tie that connects them? In their political associations, Americans of all conditions, minds, and ages acquire every day a general taste for association and grow accustomed to using it. There they meet in large numbers, they talk, they listen to each other, and they spur one another on to all sorts of undertakings. Afterward they carry the ideas they have acquired in this way into civil life and put them to a thousand uses. Thus it is by enjoying a dangerous freedom that the Americans learn the art of making the dangers of freedom less formidable.

If we pick a certain moment in the life of a nation, it is easy to prove that political associations disturb the state and paralyze productive industry. But take the whole life of a people, and it may perhaps be easy to show that freedom of association in political matters is favorable to the prosperity, and even to the tranquility, of the community.

I said in the earlier part of this work, “The unrestrained liberty of political association cannot be entirely assimilated to the liberty of the press. The one is at the same time less necessary and more dangerous than the other. A nation may confine it within certain limits without ceasing to be mistress of itself; and it may sometimes be obliged to do so in order to maintain its own authority.” And further on I added: “It cannot be denied that the unrestrained liberty of association for political purposes is the last degree of liberty which a people is fit for. If it does not throw them into anarchy, it perpetually brings them, as it were, to the verge of it.” So I do not think that a nation is always free to give its citizens an absolute right of association for political purposes. I doubt whether in any country or in any age it would be wise to set no limits to freedom of association. It is said that a certain nation could not keep the community tranquil, make the laws respected, or establish a lasting government unless the right of association were confined within narrow limits. These benefits are undoubtedly invaluable. I can imagine that, to gain or keep them, a nation may impose severe temporary restrictions on itself. Still, it is good for the nation to know at what price these benefits are bought. I can understand that it may be advisable to cut off a man’s arm to save his life. But it would be ridiculous to claim that he will be as dexterous as he was before he lost it.
